papers.limitation:
The sequence generation pipeline requires parameter fine-tuning to improve the success rate.
The features learned by the model may not directly align with manually curated dataset annotations, as latents might encode more specific or coarse-grained features.
future_direction: Extend these methods to larger models and a wider range of protein features.
Automate the parameter search for the sequence generation pipeline to improve efficiency.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancements in transformer-based language models have revolutionized natural language processing, yet understanding the internal mechanisms of these models remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to interpret the internal representations of protein language models, specifically focusing on the ESM-2 8M parameter model. By performing a statistical analysis on each latent component's relevance to distinct protein annotations, we identify potential interpretations linked to various protein characteristics, including transmembrane regions, binding sites, and specialized motifs. We then leverage these insights to guide sequence generation, shortlisting the relevant latent components that can steer the model towards desired targets such as zinc finger domains. This work contributes to the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability in biological sequence models, offering new perspectives on model steering for sequence design.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: ProtSAE: Disentangling and Interpreting Protein Language Models via Semantically-Guided Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle semantic features in protein language models to improve interpretability and enable precise model control?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ProtSAE, a semantically-guided sparse autoencoder that disentangles protein features and aligns them with biological concepts, improving interpretability and enabling steering of protein language models.
papers.conclusion: ProtSAE effectively disentangles semantic features in protein language models, leading to better interpretability and control for protein engineering tasks.
papers.key_findings:
ProtSAE learns more biologically relevant and interpretable hidden features compared to previous SAE methods.
ProtSAE maintains high reconstruction fidelity while achieving better results in interpretable probing.
ProtSAE enables effective steering of PLM outputs for downstream generation tasks.
Ablation studies show that the semantic guidance components (annotation data and domain knowledge) are crucial for performance.
papers.limitation: ProtSAE is only evaluated on ESM2 and not scaled to broader architectures or application scenarios.
future_direction: Extend ProtSAE to protein language models aligned with natural language.
Apply ProtSAE to sequence-structure co-design models.
Explore interpretable feature extraction from protein structure prediction models and generative diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) has emerged as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability of large language models. Recent works apply SAE to protein language models (PLMs), aiming to extract and analyze biologically meaningful features from their latent spaces. However, SAE suffers from semantic entanglement, where individual neurons often mix multiple nonlinear concepts, making it difficult to reliably interpret or manipulate model behaviors. In this paper, we propose a semantically-guided SAE, called ProtSAE. Unlike existing SAE which requires annotation datasets to filter and interpret activations, we guide semantic disentanglement during training using both annotation datasets and domain knowledge to mitigate the effects of entangled attributes. We design interpretability experiments showing that ProtSAE learns more biologically relevant and interpretable hidden features compared to previous methods. Performance analyses further demonstrate that ProtSAE maintains high reconstruction fidelity while achieving better results in interpretable probing. We also show the potential of ProtSAE in steering PLMs for downstream generation tasks.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders make sense of gene expression latent variable models?
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be effectively used to interpret latent representations in biological data, specifically single-cell gene expression data?
papers.core_contribution: This work explores the potential of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting latent representations in biological data, introduces scFeatureLens for automated annotation of SAE features with biological concepts, and demonstrates that SAEs can extract meaningful features that steer cells into desired biological programs.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that SAEs are a valuable tool for interpreting latent representations in biological data, and the introduced scFeatureLens pipeline provides a scalable framework for improved interpretability in single-cell analysis, though more research is needed in this field.
papers.key_findings:
Distribution type and distance of hidden generative variables affect their recovery from latent representations.
SAEs can extract meaningful features from single-cell expression models that successfully steer cells into desired programs, with features acting either locally or globally.
SAEs can uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed in traditional analysis.
The introduced automated pipeline, scFeatureLens, enables large-scale interpretability analysis by linking SAE features to biological concepts from gene sets.
SAEs do not provide an advantage over simple baselines for recovering known features, but are valuable for discovering unknown features and data generation structure.
papers.limitation:
Variables with an indirect effect on the observed data and little structure in the generative process could practically not be recovered.
SAEs do not pose an advantage in the recovery of known or hypothesized features compared to simple baselines.
The case study was limited to Gene Ontology terms which are incomplete and biased towards well-studied genes.
future_direction: Future work could explore metrics for evaluating the biological meaningfulness in and differences between embeddings.
More research is needed in the field of interpretability for biological models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have lately been used to uncover interpretable latent features in large language models. By projecting dense embeddings into a much higher-dimensional and sparse space, learned features become disentangled and easier to interpret. This work explores the potential of SAEs for decomposing embeddings in complex and high-dimensional biological data. Using simulated data, it outlines the efficacy, hyperparameter landscape, and limitations of SAEs when it comes to extracting ground truth generative variables from latent space. The application to embeddings from pretrained single-cell models shows that SAEs can find and steer key biological processes and even uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed. This work further introduces scFeatureLens, an automated interpretability approach for linking SAE features and biological concepts from gene sets to enable large-scale analysis and hypothesis generation in single-cell gene expression models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable Structure in Small Gene Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, revealing features like nucleotide identity and transcription factor binding motifs, demonstrating that compact models learn structured genomic representations.
papers.conclusion: SAEs can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, highlighting their ability to capture essential genomic features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs extracted sparse features corresponding to individual nucleotides with high precision.
SAEs identified features aligned with known transcription factor binding motifs, such as MA1596.1 and MA0052.5.
Even compact models effectively capture transcription factor binding specificity.
The recall variability indicates the complexity and redundancy of regulatory elements in genomic sequences.
future_direction: Extend SAE approach to other genomic contexts like non-coding regions or species-specific variations.
Explore SAEs for model refinement and interpretability across different architectures.
Apply SAEs to other biological modalities like single-cell gene expression and multi-omics datasets.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), revealing latent latent features with semantical meaning. This interpretability has also proven valuable in biological domains: applying SAEs to protein language models uncovered meaningful features related to protein structure and function. More recently, SAEs have been used to analyze genomics-focused models such as Evo 2, identifying interpretable features in gene sequences. However, it remains unclear whether SAEs can extract meaningful representations from small gene language models, which have fewer parameters and potentially less expressive capacity. To address it, we propose applying SAEs to the activations of a small gene language model. We demonstrate that even small-scale models encode biologically relevant genomic features, such as transcription factor binding motifs, that SAEs can effectively uncover. Our findings suggest that compact gene language models are capable of learning structured genomic representations, and that SAEs offer a scalable approach for interpreting gene models across various model sizes.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) truly uncover all concepts a model relies on, or are they inherently biased toward certain kinds of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a duality framework between SAE architectures and concept geometry, showing that SAEs impose implicit assumptions about concept structure, and proposes a new SAE (SpaDE) that explicitly incorporates nonlinear separability and concept heterogeneity to recover previously hidden concepts.
papers.conclusion: There is no universal SAE architecture; the choice of SAE should be guided by the geometry of concepts in the model's representations, and data-aware design is essential for effective interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are not universal; their architecture imposes implicit assumptions about concept structure (e.g., linear separability, uniform dimensionality) that bias what they can detect.
Existing SAEs (ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK) fail to recover concepts that are nonlinearly separable or have heterogeneous intrinsic dimensionality.
The proposed SpaDE SAE, which uses a sparsemax projection and Euclidean distances, can adaptively capture concepts with nonlinear separability and heterogeneous dimensionality.
Experiments on synthetic data, formal languages, and vision activations validate that SpaDE discovers concepts missed by other SAEs and maintains clearer concept boundaries.
The duality between SAE architecture and concept geometry suggests that interpretability tools must be designed with the data's concept structure in mind.
papers.limitation:
SpaDE assumes that Euclidean distances are meaningful in the concept space, which may not hold for all datasets.
The duality framework currently covers ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, and SpaDE, but may not generalize to all SAE variants.
Experiments are limited to synthetic data, a formal language, and one vision dataset (Imagenette); broader validation is needed.
future_direction: Extend the duality framework to other SAE architectures and interpretability methods.
Automate the selection of SAE architecture based on data properties.
Explore more complex concept structures beyond nonlinear separability and heterogeneity.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret neural networks by identifying meaningful concepts from their representations. However, do SAEs truly uncover all concepts a model relies on, or are they inherently biased toward certain kinds of concepts? We introduce a unified framework that recasts SAEs as solutions to a bilevel optimization problem, revealing a fundamental challenge: each SAE imposes structural assumptions about how concepts are encoded in model representations, which in turn shapes what it can and cannot detect. This means different SAEs are not interchangeable -- switching architectures can expose entirely new concepts or obscure existing ones. To systematically probe this effect, we evaluate SAEs across a spectrum of settings: from controlled toy models that isolate key variables, to semi-synthetic experiments on real model activations and finally to large-scale, naturalistic datasets. Across this progression, we examine two fundamental properties that real-world concepts often exhibit: heterogeneity in intrinsic dimensionality (some concepts are inherently low-dimensional, others are not) and nonlinear separability. We show that SAEs fail to recover concepts when these properties are ignored, and we design a new SAE that explicitly incorporates both, enabling the discovery of previously hidden concepts and reinforcing our theoretical insights. Our findings challenge the idea of a universal SAE and underscores the need for architecture-specific choices in model interpretability. Overall, we argue an SAE does not just reveal concepts -- it determines what can be seen at all.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can find a canonical set of units of analysis (unique, complete, and atomic features) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis because smaller SAEs are incomplete (missing information) and larger SAEs learn composed, non-atomic features. The choice of SAE dictionary size should be pragmatic.
papers.conclusion: Alternative methods are required for identifying canonical units of analysis, and SAE practitioners should adopt a pragmatic approach to choosing dictionary size for interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE stitching reveals that larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve reconstruction when added to smaller SAEs, indicating smaller SAEs are incomplete.
SAE stitching shows that larger SAEs also contain reconstruction latents similar to those in smaller SAEs, but sometimes composed of multiple smaller latents.
Meta-SAEs can decompose larger SAE latents into interpretable meta-latents, demonstrating that larger SAE latents are not atomic.
Meta-latents are similar to latents found in smaller SAEs, suggesting larger SAE latents are compositions of smaller SAE latents.
The sparsity penalty in SAEs incentivizes the learning of composed features in larger dictionaries, rather than atomic features.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines two language models (GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B) and does not include very large SAEs.
Associating SAE latents with interpretable concepts remains an open problem, and the methods do not identify canonical units nor the optimal dictionary size.
future_direction: Pursue different approaches for identifying canonical units of analysis.
Pragmatically choose SAE dictionary size based on the specific interpretability task.
papers.abstract: A common goal of mechanistic interpretability is to decompose the activations of neural networks into features: interpretable properties of the input computed by the model. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for finding these features in LLMs, and it has been postulated that they can be used to find a \textit{canonical} set of units: a unique and complete list of atomic features. We cast doubt on this belief using two novel techniques: SAE stitching to show they are incomplete, and meta-SAEs to show they are not atomic. SAE stitching involves inserting or swapping latents from a larger SAE into a smaller one. Latents from the larger SAE can be divided into two categories: \emph{novel latents}, which improve performance when added to the smaller SAE, indicating they capture novel information, and \emph{reconstruction latents}, which can replace corresponding latents in the smaller SAE that have similar behavior. The existence of novel features indicates incompleteness of smaller SAEs. Using meta-SAEs -- SAEs trained on the decoder matrix of another SAE -- we find that latents in SAEs often decompose into combinations of latents from a smaller SAE, showing that larger SAE latents are not atomic. The resulting decompositions are often interpretable; e.g. a latent representing ``Einstein'' decomposes into ``scientist'', ``Germany'', and ``famous person''. Even if SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis, they may still be useful tools. We suggest that future research should either pursue different approaches for identifying such units, or pragmatically choose the SAE size suited to their task. We provide an interactive dashboard to explore meta-SAEs: https://metasaes.streamlit.app/

papers.title: PolySAE: Modeling Feature Interactions in Sparse Autoencoders via Polynomial Decoding
papers.research_question: How can we extend sparse autoencoders to model non-linear feature interactions (compositional structure) while preserving a linear encoder for interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PolySAE, a sparse autoencoder that extends the decoder with quadratic and cubic terms to model feature interactions via low-rank tensor factorization, improving feature separation and probing performance while maintaining reconstruction fidelity.
papers.conclusion: PolySAE effectively models feature interactions in sparse autoencoders, capturing compositional structure beyond linear combinations and improving interpretability without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
papers.key_findings:
PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 across four language models and three SAE variants while maintaining comparable reconstruction error.
PolySAE produces 2–10× larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions, indicating more separated semantic structure.
Learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency (r=0.06), suggesting they capture compositional structure rather than surface statistics.
PolySAE adds a small parameter overhead (3% for GPT-2 small) through low-rank factorization of interaction terms.
Qualitative analysis shows PolySAE captures compositional structures like morphological binding (e.g., 'administrators') and phrasal composition (e.g., 'Starbucks').
papers.limitation: The study is limited to models up to 2B parameters and experiments are restricted to forced-sparsity SAE variants.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method for interpreting neural network representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of dictionary atoms. However, SAEs assume that features combine additively through linear reconstruction, an assumption that cannot capture compositional structure: linear models cannot distinguish whether "Starbucks" arises from the composition of "star" and "coffee" features or merely their co-occurrence. This forces SAEs to allocate monolithic features for compound concepts rather than decomposing them into interpretable constituents. We introduce PolySAE, which extends the SAE decoder with higher-order terms to model feature interactions while preserving the linear encoder essential for interpretability. Through low-rank tensor factorization on a shared projection subspace, PolySAE captures pairwise and triple feature interactions with small parameter overhead (3% on GPT2). Across four language models and three SAE variants, PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 while maintaining comparable reconstruction error, and produces 2-10$\times$ larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions. Critically, learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency ($r = 0.06$ vs. $r = 0.82$ for SAE feature covariance), suggesting that polynomial terms capture compositional structure, such as morphological binding and phrasal composition, largely independent of surface statistics.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Low-$N$ Protein Function Prediction and Design
papers.research_question: How effective are sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for protein function prediction and design in low-data (low-N) regimes?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a compact and biologically meaningful latent space that improves low-N fitness prediction and enables effective protein design via latent steering, outperforming ESM2 baselines.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a powerful tool for low-N protein function prediction and design, expanding the biologist's toolkit for resource-constrained applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform ESM2 baselines in 58% of fitness extrapolation tasks with as few as 24 training sequences.
SAEs design top-fitness variants in 83% of cases via latent steering, compared to designing with ESM2 alone.
The sparse latent space of SAEs encodes biologically interpretable motifs and compresses relevant information, reducing overfitting in low-N regimes.
Analysis of steered variants reveals that SAEs activate latents corresponding to known biological motifs such as active sites, allosteric sites, and epistatic sites.
SAE performance is influenced by the number of available multiple sequence alignment (MSA) sequences for training.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to a set of proteins; it could be extended to other proteins with clinically relevant functions such as antibiotic resistance and viral replication.
SAE performance is strongly influenced by the number of MSA sequences available for training; strategies are needed for robust training when MSAs are shallow.
Protein engineering experiments rely on in-silico fitness models; wet lab validation is necessary to verify function.
Designed variants are constrained to a maximum of five mutations away from the wildtype; beyond this radius, designing highly-functional sequences is difficult with a single predictive latent.
In-silico evaluation tools become less reliable the further away variants are from the wildtype.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to other proteins with clinically relevant functions.
Explore strategies for robust SAE training when multiple sequence alignments are shallow or unavailable.
Couple SAE steering with physics-based tools like Rosetta to jointly optimize for both function and stability.
papers.abstract: Predicting protein function from amino acid sequence remains a central challenge in data-scarce (low-$N$) regimes, limiting machine learning-guided protein design when only small amounts of assay-labeled sequence-function data are available. Protein language models (pLMs) have advanced the field by providing evolutionary-informed embeddings and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled decomposition of these embeddings into interpretable latent variables that capture structural and functional features. However, the effectiveness of SAEs for low-$N$ function prediction and protein design has not been systematically studied. Herein, we evaluate SAEs trained on fine-tuned ESM2 embeddings across diverse fitness extrapolation and protein engineering tasks. We show that SAEs, with as few as 24 sequences, consistently outperform or compete with their ESM2 baselines in fitness prediction, indicating that their sparse latent space encodes compact and biologically meaningful representations that generalize more effectively from limited data. Moreover, steering predictive latents exploits biological motifs in pLM representations, yielding top-fitness variants in 83% of cases compared to designing with ESM2 alone.

papers.title: Explainable Molecular Property Prediction: Aligning Chemical Concepts with Predictions via Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property predictions using language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Lamole, a framework for explainable molecular property prediction that uses Group SELFIES representation and combines attention weights with gradients, calibrated by a marginal loss, to provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Lamole provides chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property prediction and can be integrated into an interpretable optimization pipeline for molecular design.
papers.key_findings:
Lamole achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art baselines while improving explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%.
The proposed information flow-based explanation method, integrating attention and gradients, captures interactions between functional groups.
The marginal loss aligns explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, ensuring concept-aligned results.
Using only 10% of molecules with ground truth annotations can significantly improve explanation accuracy.
Integration with an evolutionary algorithm demonstrates Lamole's actionable utility for guiding molecular editing and optimization.
papers.limitation:
Complex interactions caused by multiple functional groups may not be fully captured, and other functional groups may receive relatively high importance scores.
The molecular editing case is a computational demonstration and does not imply real-world chemical optimality.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader generalization scenarios, including unseen chemotypes.
Designing more strategies to reveal complex functional group interactions.
papers.abstract: Providing explainable molecular property predictions is critical for many scientific domains, such as drug discovery and material science. Though transformer-based language models have shown great potential in accurate molecular property prediction, they neither provide chemically meaningful explanations nor faithfully reveal the molecular structure-property relationships. In this work, we develop a framework for explainable molecular property prediction based on language models, dubbed as Lamole, which can provide chemical concepts-aligned explanations. We take a string-based molecular representation -- Group SELFIES -- as input tokens to pretrain and fine-tune our Lamole, as it provides chemically meaningful semantics. By disentangling the information flows of Lamole, we propose combining self-attention weights and gradients for better quantification of each chemically meaningful substructure's impact on the model's output. To make the explanations more faithfully respect the structure-property relationship, we then carefully craft a marginal loss to explicitly optimize the explanations to be able to align with the chemists' annotations. We bridge the manifold hypothesis with the elaborated marginal loss to prove that the loss can align the explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, leading to concept-aligned explanations. Experimental results over six mutagenicity datasets and one hepatotoxicity dataset demonstrate Lamole can achieve comparable classification accuracy and boost the explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%, being the state-of-the-art in explainable molecular property prediction.

papers.title: Evaluating Open-Source Sparse Autoencoders on Disentangling Factual Knowledge in GPT-2 Small
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature spaces are useful for causal interpretability analysis, specifically for disentangling related factual knowledge (country and continent of cities) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: Current open-source sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for GPT-2 small struggle to provide a feature space that better disentangles factual knowledge than the baseline of neurons, and none approach the performance of the supervised DAS skyline.
papers.conclusion: Only one of the evaluated SAEs reached the neuron baseline and none reached the DAS skyline, indicating current SAEs are not superior to neurons for this causal disentanglement task, but the evaluation is a useful step for assessing SAEs in interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Using representations reconstructed by SAEs degrades the model's knowledge of cities.
The end-to-end SAEs degrade knowledge less relative to their reconstruction loss, but this is weak evidence.
There is a significant gap between the neuron baseline and the DAS skyline, showing neurons can be improved upon.
Current SAEs for GPT-2 small generally perform below the neuron baseline, with only the top-k Open AI SAE matching it.
The top-k SAE (Open AI SAE) is the most performant among the evaluated SAEs.
papers.limitation: The evaluation is limited to GPT-2 small and a specific dataset (cities, countries, continents). Future work should scale to larger models and more attributes.
future_direction: Scale experiments to models with available SAEs including gemma, Mistral, Llama, and Pythia.
Use more attributes from the RA VEL dataset, such as language, gender, etc., for larger models with more knowledge.
papers.abstract: A popular new method in mechanistic interpretability is to train high-dimensional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on neuron activations and use SAE features as the atomic units of analysis. However, the body of evidence on whether SAE feature spaces are useful for causal analysis is underdeveloped. In this work, we use the RAVEL benchmark to evaluate whether SAEs trained on hidden representations of GPT-2 small have sets of features that separately mediate knowledge of which country a city is in and which continent it is in. We evaluate four open-source SAEs for GPT-2 small against each other, with neurons serving as a baseline, and linear features learned via distributed alignment search (DAS) serving as a skyline. For each, we learn a binary mask to select features that will be patched to change the country of a city without changing the continent, or vice versa. Our results show that SAEs struggle to reach the neuron baseline, and none come close to the DAS skyline. We release code here: https://github.com/MaheepChaudhary/SAE-Ravel

papers.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How does the L0 hyperparameter (average number of active features per token) in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) affect the quality of learned features, and how can the correct L0 be determined?
papers.core_contribution: The L0 hyperparameter in Sparse Autoencoders must be set correctly to learn monosemantic features; if L0 is too low or too high, the SAE mixes correlated features, and the paper provides a proxy metric (decoder pairwise cosine similarity) to guide L0 selection.
papers.conclusion: The L0 hyperparameter must be set correctly for SAEs to learn correct, monosemantic features, and most existing SAEs likely have an L0 that is too low.
papers.key_findings:
If L0 is set too low, SAEs mix positively correlated features to improve reconstruction, leading to polysemantic latents.
If L0 is set too high, SAEs find degenerate solutions that also mix features.
Commonly used sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots are not a sound evaluation method, as they can favor incorrect SAEs that mix features over a ground-truth SAE.
A proxy metric, decoder pairwise cosine similarity (c_dec), is minimized when the SAE L0 matches the true underlying L0 of the data distribution.
Most commonly used open-source SAEs have an L0 that is too low.
papers.limitation:
The investigation is limited to features satisfying the linear representation hypothesis and does not consider non-linear underlying features.
The study only investigated a few layers of popular LLMs due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Investigate how SAEs react if the underlying features are non-linear.
Explore the impact of different correlation structures (e.g., unbalanced correlations) on SAEs.
Extend the analysis to more layers of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) extract features from LLM internal activations, meant to correspond to interpretable concepts. A core SAE training hyperparameter is L0: how many SAE features should fire per token on average. Existing work compares SAE algorithms using sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots, implying L0 is a free parameter with no single correct value aside from its effect on reconstruction. In this work we study the effect of L0 on SAEs, and show that if L0 is not set correctly, the SAE fails to disentangle the underlying features of the LLM. If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that L0 must be set correctly to train SAEs with correct features.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn meaningful feature decompositions of neural network activations, or can their performance be matched by random baselines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) fail to reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms, as they recover very few ground-truth features in synthetic experiments and are matched in performance by simple random baselines on real model activations.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE evaluation practices are insufficient, and SAEs in their present state do not reliably learn meaningful feature decompositions. The proposed random baselines serve as simple sanity checks for future work.
papers.key_findings:
In synthetic experiments with known ground-truth features, SAEs recover only 9% of true features despite achieving 71% explained variance, showing a disconnect between reconstruction and feature recovery.
Three random baselines (Frozen Decoder, Soft-Frozen Decoder, Frozen Encoder) match fully-trained SAEs across key evaluation metrics: interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72).
In the synthetic variable probability setting, SAEs recover only the highest-frequency ground-truth features, leaving over 90% of the feature dictionary unmatched.
The reconstruction objective is a poor proxy for meaningful decomposition, as SAEs can achieve strong reconstruction without aligning with true features.
The competitive performance of frozen baselines suggests SAEs may operate in a 'lazy training' regime, achieving most gains through minimal adjustments to randomly initialized components.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic experiment assumes independent feature activations, omitting correlations that likely exist in real neural networks.
The work focuses on standard SAE architectures and does not evaluate related approaches such as transcoders or crosscoders.
future_direction: Explore objectives that more directly incentivize feature alignment rather than just reconstruction.
Design appropriate randomization baselines for related methods like transcoders and crosscoders.
Incorporate more realistic feature dependencies in synthetic evaluation setups.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders: From Shallow Design to Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the limitations of shallow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in extracting correlated features due to an implicit quasi-orthogonality assumption, and proposes an iterative SAE based on Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE) to overcome these limitations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, an iterative sparse autoencoder that unrolls Matching Pursuit, which improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs by enabling residual-guided extraction of correlated features.
papers.conclusion: MP-SAE improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs, providing a foundation for building more interpretable sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
MP-SAE is more expressive than shallow SAEs across varying sparsity levels and dictionary sizes.
MP-SAE learns a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine feature structure, with early atoms capturing digit prototypes and later atoms refining pen strokes.
MP-SAE learns a globally coherent dictionary but selects more incoherent subsets of atoms during inference, unlike shallow SAEs where dictionary and selected atom coherence align.
MP-SAE guarantees monotonic improvement in reconstruction as more atoms are selected, a property not shared by other SAEs.
Shallow SAEs (ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, BatchTopK) exhibit distinct structural biases in their learned dictionaries, such as ReLU learning full-digit atoms and others learning pen-stroke patterns.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently become central tools for interpretability, leveraging dictionary learning principles to extract sparse, interpretable features from neural representations whose underlying structure is typically unknown. This paper evaluates SAEs in a controlled setting using MNIST, which reveals that current shallow architectures implicitly rely on a quasi-orthogonality assumption that limits the ability to extract correlated features. To move beyond this, we compare them with an iterative SAE that unrolls Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE), enabling the residual-guided extraction of correlated features that arise in hierarchical settings such as handwritten digit generation while guaranteeing monotonic improvement of the reconstruction as more atoms are selected.

papers.title: Use Sparse Autoencoders to Discover Unknown Concepts, Not to Act on Known Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we reconcile conflicting narratives about the usefulness of sparse autoencoders (SAEs)? The paper argues that SAEs are less effective for acting on known concepts but powerful for discovering unknown concepts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a conceptual distinction: SAEs are less effective for acting on known concepts but powerful for discovering unknown concepts. It outlines use cases for SAEs in ML interpretability, fairness, auditing, safety, and social/health sciences.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that successful uses of SAEs involve discovering unknown concepts, and this distinction highlights the potential of SAEs for various research areas.
papers.key_findings:
Negative results on SAEs pertain to tasks that act on known concepts, such as concept detection and model steering, where SAEs underperform simple baselines.
Positive results on SAEs involve discovering unknown concepts, such as in hypothesis generation and explaining language model outputs (biology of LLMs).
SAEs can bridge the prediction-explanation gap by converting black box representations into interpretable natural language concepts.
SAEs are a promising tool for applications in ML interpretability, fairness, auditing, safety, and social/health sciences.
future_direction: Using SAEs for ML fairness, interpretability, explainability, auditing, and safety.
Using SAEs in social and health sciences to discover unknown concepts from text data.
Bridging the prediction-explanation gap with SAEs.
papers.abstract: While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have generated significant excitement, a series of negative results have added to skepticism about their usefulness. Here, we establish a conceptual distinction that reconciles competing narratives surrounding SAEs. We argue that while SAEs may be less effective for acting on known concepts, SAEs are powerful tools for discovering unknown concepts. This distinction cleanly separates existing negative and positive results, and suggests several classes of SAE applications. Specifically, we outline use cases for SAEs in (i) ML interpretability, explainability, fairness, auditing, and safety, and (ii) social and health sciences.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
papers.research_question: How can feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be achieved and measured to improve the reliability of mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and proposes the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to measure consistency. It shows that high consistency is achievable with appropriate architectural choices (e.g., TopK SAEs) and that high PW-MCC correlates with semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.conclusion: The paper calls for a community-wide shift towards valuing and systematically measuring feature consistency in SAEs for cumulative progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
High feature consistency (PW-MCC ≈ 0.80) is achievable with TopK SAEs on real-world LLM activations.
PW-MCC reliably tracks ground-truth feature recovery (GT-MCC) in synthetic experiments.
Feature consistency is frequency-dependent: more frequent features are learned more consistently.
Different SAE architectures yield different levels of consistency, with TopK SAEs performing best.
High PW-MCC scores correlate strongly with the semantic similarity of feature explanations.
papers.limitation:
The focus is on SAEs, and other interpretability methods may have different consistency challenges.
The study uses a specific metric (PW-MCC) for a specific notion of consistency (strong feature consistency).
The real-world experiments are limited to two base models and one dataset.
The automated interpretation pipeline has its own limitations.
future_direction: Extending consistency analysis to other interpretability methods beyond SAEs.
Developing more nuanced metrics for consistency that go beyond strong feature consistency.
Investigating the relationship between consistency and downstream task performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.

papers.title: Attribute Graphs Underlying Molecular Generative Models: Path to Learning with Limited Data
papers.research_question: How can we extract a graphical model (attribute graph) relating data attributes from the latent representations of a pre-trained generative model, and use this structure for robust prediction with limited out-of-distribution data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PerturbLearn, a method to extract an attribute graph (a DAG) from a pre-trained generative autoencoder by perturbing latent codes and observing influences on data attributes, and shows that using the Markov blanket from this graph for feature selection leads to robust prediction under distribution shifts with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The PerturbLearn framework successfully extracts a graphical model from a pre-trained generative model, and using this structure for feature selection enables more robust and generalizable predictors in scenarios with limited out-of-distribution data.
papers.key_findings:
The attribute graph derived by PerturbLearn captures latent-mediated influences among molecular attributes.
Predictors using the Markov blanket features from the PerturbLearn graph show better generalization and robustness to distribution shifts, especially when fine-tuning data is limited (e.g., n=7, 10, 25 samples).
The method is competitive with or outperforms existing causal discovery (GES, LiNGAM) and feature selection methods (Sparse Group Lasso, PPFS) in low-data regimes across multiple pharmacokinetic property prediction tasks.
The derived graphical model provides a means for sample-efficient domain adaptation and offers (partial) interpretability by identifying relevant attributes.
papers.limitation: Dependency on a pre-determined set of data attributes, which may not be comprehensive.
future_direction: Further investigation on the accordance of the derived attribute graph with domain priors.
Using only low-level and cheaply computable attributes.
Incorporating expert knowledge.
papers.abstract: Training generative models that capture rich semantics of the data and interpreting the latent representations encoded by such models are very important problems in un-/self-supervised learning. In this work, we provide a simple algorithm that relies on perturbation experiments on latent codes of a pre-trained generative autoencoder to uncover an attribute graph that is implied by the generative model. We perform perturbation experiments to check for influence of a given latent variable on a subset of attributes. Given this, we show that one can fit an effective graphical model that models a structural equation model between latent codes taken as exogenous variables and attributes taken as observed variables. One interesting aspect is that a single latent variable controls multiple overlapping subsets of attributes unlike conventional approaches that try to impose full independence. Using a pre-trained generative autoencoder trained on a large dataset of small molecules, we demonstrate that the graphical model between various molecular attributes and latent codes learned by our algorithm can be used to predict a specific property for molecules which are drawn from a different distribution. We compare prediction models trained on various feature subsets chosen by simple baselines, as well as existing causal discovery and sparse learning/feature selection methods, with the ones in the derived Markov blanket from our method. Results show empirically that the predictor that relies on our Markov blanket attributes is robust to distribution shifts when transferred or fine-tuned with a few samples from the new distribution, especially when training data is limited.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
