papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
papers.research_question: How can we control fine-grained reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models using Sparse Autoencoders to overcome concept entanglement and improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-Steering, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle and identify strategy-specific features for controlling reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models, achieving superior control effectiveness and error correction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can disentangle strategy-specific features for fine-grained control of reasoning strategies, with SAE-Steering providing an efficient feature identification pipeline that is effective and robust.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Steering outperforms existing control methods by over 15% in control effectiveness across various reasoning tasks and models.
The identified SAE features generalize from math to science domains, indicating cross-domain applicability.
Logit-based feature recall is more precise than activation-based methods, improving feature selection accuracy.
Strategy-specific features are prevalent in deeper layers of the model, with optimal control effectiveness in middle-to-late layers.
Controlling reasoning strategies can redirect models from erroneous paths, achieving a 7% absolute accuracy improvement in error correction.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated five representative reasoning strategies
Only demonstrated application in error correction scenarios
Only attempted to correct erroneous paths by enforcing continued reasoning
future_direction: Investigate controlling other reasoning strategies
Explore applying control to a wider range of applications
Explore guiding the LRM at earlier stages or during intermediate steps
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit human-like cognitive reasoning strategies (e.g. backtracking, cross-verification) during reasoning process, which improves their performance on complex tasks. Currently, reasoning strategies are autonomously selected by LRMs themselves. However, such autonomous selection often produces inefficient or even erroneous reasoning paths. To make reasoning more reliable and flexible, it is important to develop methods for controlling reasoning strategies. Existing methods struggle to control fine-grained reasoning strategies due to conceptual entanglement in LRMs' hidden states. To address this, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose strategy-entangled hidden states into a disentangled feature space. To identify the few strategy-specific features from the vast pool of SAE features, we propose SAE-Steering, an efficient two-stage feature identification pipeline. SAE-Steering first recalls features that amplify the logits of strategy-specific keywords, filtering out over 99\% of features, and then ranks the remaining features by their control effectiveness. Using the identified strategy-specific features as control vectors, SAE-Steering outperforms existing methods by over 15\% in control effectiveness. Furthermore, controlling reasoning strategies can redirect LRMs from erroneous paths to correct ones, achieving a 7\% absolute accuracy improvement.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: What can attribution methods show us about chemical language models?
papers.research_question: How can attribution methods be used to explain the predictions of a chemical language model for aqueous solubility?
papers.core_contribution: The adapted transformer-specific attribution method produces sparse attributions that reflect how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, while SHAP provides sensible atom-level attributions but fails to explain functional groups relevant to solubility.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods provide insight into how chemical language models represent molecules, but current techniques have limitations in explaining solubility predictions in terms of functional groups, instead revealing how the model organizes its latent space.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning the MegaMolBART encoder significantly improves aqueous solubility prediction accuracy.
The transformer-specific attribution method (using the hRi token) yields sparse attributions that are characteristic of how the model represents molecular similarity in its latent space.
SHAP provides chemically sensible attributions (e.g., highlighting electronegative atoms) but does not explain predictions at the level of functional groups.
The fine-tuned model's latent space becomes linearly separable with respect to solubility along the first principal component.
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, limiting its ability to attribute negative contributions to solubility.
papers.limitation:
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, preventing attribution of features that negatively contribute to solubility.
SHAP does not capture functional group-level explanations for solubility predictions.
ECFP-based models are less predictive and their explanations are coarse-grained.
future_direction: Using the attributions to design focused, informative chemical datasets by creating training examples that contravene the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Language models trained on molecular string representations have shown strong performance in predictive and generative tasks. However, practical applications require not only making accurate predictions, but also explainability - the ability to explain the reasons and rationale behind the predictions. In this work, we explore explainability for a chemical language model by adapting a transformer-specific and a model-agnostic input attribution technique. We fine-tune a pretrained model to predict aqueous solubility, compare training and architecture variants, and evaluate visualizations of attributed relevance. The model-agnostic SHAP technique provides sensible attributions, highlighting the positive influence of individual electronegative atoms, but does not explain the model in terms of functional groups or explain how the model represents molecular strings internally to make predictions. In contrast, the adapted transformer-specific explainability technique produces sparse attributions, which cannot be directly attributed to functional groups relevant to solubility. Instead, the attributions are more characteristic of how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, which seems to represent features relevant to molecular similarity rather than functional groups. These findings provide insight into the representations underpinning chemical language models, which we propose may be leveraged for the design of informative chemical spaces for training more accurate, advanced and explainable models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Features for Classifications and Transferability
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features be effectively used for interpretable classification in safety-critical tasks, and what is their performance in cross-lingual and cross-modal transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic analysis of SAE features for interpretable classification, showing that binarized SAE features outperform hidden-state and bag-of-words baselines and demonstrate robust cross-lingual and cross-modal transferability.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are effective for interpretable classification and transfer across languages and modalities, establishing new best practices for SAE-based interpretability in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-derived features achieve macro F1 > 0.8, outperforming hidden-state and bag-of-words baselines.
SAE features show cross-model transfer from Gemma 2 2B to 9B-IT models.
SAE features generalize in a zero-shot manner to cross-lingual toxicity detection and visual classification tasks.
Binarization offers an efficient alternative to traditional feature selection while maintaining or improving performance.
Middle-layer SAE features typically yield the highest classification performance.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is limited to Gemma 2 models and a specific set of safety-oriented tasks; robustness under adversarial conditions or domain shifts needs further study.
The semantic alignment of SAE features with human-interpretable concepts remains an open question.
The toxicity or other safety-related open-sourced data used contained offensive language.
future_direction: Investigate robustness under domain shift, including covariate, subpopulation, and temporal shifts.
Expand the task set beyond safety-oriented binary classification to include multilabel and non-safety tasks and additional multilingual benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide potentials for uncovering structured, human-interpretable representations in Large Language Models (LLMs), making them a crucial tool for transparent and controllable AI systems. We systematically analyze SAE for interpretable feature extraction from LLMs in safety-critical classification tasks. Our framework evaluates (1) model-layer selection and scaling properties, (2) SAE architectural configurations, including width and pooling strategies, and (3) the effect of binarizing continuous SAE activations. SAE-derived features achieve macro F1 > 0.8, outperforming hidden-state and BoW baselines while demonstrating cross-model transfer from Gemma 2 2B to 9B-IT models. These features generalize in a zero-shot manner to cross-lingual toxicity detection and visual classification tasks. Our analysis highlights the significant impact of pooling strategies and binarization thresholds, showing that binarization offers an efficient alternative to traditional feature selection while maintaining or improving performance. These findings establish new best practices for SAE-based interpretability and enable scalable, transparent deployment of LLMs in real-world applications. Full repo: https://github.com/shan23chen/MOSAIC.

papers.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can we identify functionally important features in neural networks? The paper investigates whether standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn features that are functionally important for network performance and proposes a new training method to ensure the features are functionally important.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces end-to-end sparse dictionary learning, a method for training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that ensures the learned features are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted.
papers.conclusion: End-to-end sparse dictionary learning offers a Pareto improvement over standard SAEs, requiring fewer features to explain network performance without sacrificing interpretability, bringing us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately.
papers.key_findings:
For the same level of performance explained, end-to-end SAEs require activating more than twice as few features per datapoint compared to standard SAEs.
End-to-end SAEs require fewer total features over the dataset to explain the same amount of network performance.
End-to-end SAEs with downstream reconstruction loss (SAEe2e+ds) achieve similar performance to SAEe2e while having activations that follow more similar pathways through the network compared to the original model.
The improved efficiency of end-to-end SAEs does not come at the cost of interpretability, as measured by automated interpretability scores and qualitative analysis.
End-to-end SAEs have more orthogonal features and are less prone to feature splitting compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation:
End-to-end SAEs take 2-3.5 times longer to train than standard SAEs.
There is a risk that SAEe2e may take different computational pathways through the network, though this is addressed by SAEe2e+ds.
The automated interpretability score is an imperfect metric of interpretability.
future_direction: Using training tweaks such as a sparsity schedule to allow for higher learning rates.
Using locally trained SAEs as initializations to reduce training time.
Training multiple SAEs at different layers concurrently to reduce training time.
papers.abstract: Identifying the features learned by neural networks is a core challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse, overcomplete dictionary that reconstructs a network's internal activations, have been used to identify these features. However, SAEs may learn more about the structure of the datatset than the computational structure of the network. There is therefore only indirect reason to believe that the directions found in these dictionaries are functionally important to the network. We propose end-to-end (e2e) sparse dictionary learning, a method for training SAEs that ensures the features learned are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted. Compared to standard SAEs, e2e SAEs offer a Pareto improvement: They explain more network performance, require fewer total features, and require fewer simultaneously active features per datapoint, all with no cost to interpretability. We explore geometric and qualitative differences between e2e SAE features and standard SAE features. E2e dictionary learning brings us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately. We release our library for training e2e SAEs and reproducing our analysis at https://github.com/ApolloResearch/e2e_sae

papers.title: Applying sparse autoencoders to unlearn knowledge in language models
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models in an interpretable way.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that individual interpretable SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models, but current SAE quality or intervention techniques result in similar or larger side-effects than fine-tuning based methods like Representation Misdirection for Unlearning (RMU).
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning is possible but currently has limitations; improvements in SAE quality or intervention techniques are needed to make it comparable to fine-tuning based techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models.
Negative scaling of feature activations is necessary for unlearning; zero ablating features is ineffective.
Intervening on multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
The specific decoder vectors are important for unlearning in gemma-2-2b-it, but not as critical in gemma-2b-it.
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, not the weights, so the original knowledge remains in the weights.
papers.limitation:
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, without modifying the model weights, so the original knowledge is still contained in the weights.
Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.
SAE-based unlearning results in similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
future_direction: Examine how SAE quality and width impact unlearning effectiveness.
Compare SAE-based unlearning to activation steering using bio-related and non-bio-related prompt pairs.
Investigate how SAE interventions affect related features in subsequent layers to better understand the unlearning mechanism.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models. We use the biology subset of the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy dataset and test on the gemma-2b-it and gemma-2-2b-it language models. We demonstrate that individual interpretable biology-related SAE features can be used to unlearn a subset of WMDP-Bio questions with minimal side-effects in domains other than biology. Our results suggest that negative scaling of feature activations is necessary and that zero ablating features is ineffective. We find that intervening using multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple different topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing Representation Misdirection for Unlearning technique. Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.

papers.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the amortisation gap in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and can more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that sparse autoencoder (SAE) encoders are inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference due to an amortisation gap, and demonstrates empirically that more expressive encoders (like MLPs) and sparse coding methods can outperform SAEs, leading to more interpretable features in large language models.
papers.conclusion: More sophisticated sparse inference methods, such as MLPs and sparse coding, can outperform traditional SAE encoders, reducing the amortisation gap and improving interpretability, which opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAE encoders have a provable amortisation gap, making them suboptimal for sparse inference even in solvable cases.
Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and sparse coding consistently outperform SAEs in recovering sparse codes, with sparse coding achieving the highest performance.
The performance advantage of more sophisticated methods is more pronounced in regimes where compressed sensing theory predicts recoverability.
These findings generalize to real-world applications, as shown by training on GPT-2 activations where MLPs yield more interpretable features than SAEs.
The amortisation gap can be reduced with increased compute, with MLPs surpassing SAE performance after a consistent computational threshold.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result on SAE suboptimality is proven for a specific setting (linear-nonlinear encoder, sparse signals in union of subspaces) and may not cover all practical SAE implementations.
future_direction: Pitting optimised sparse coding approaches (e.g., Least Angle Regression, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) against optimised SAE architectures.
Further exploration of top-k sparse coding with proper hyperparameter tuning to achieve Pareto improvements.
Scaling the methods to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

papers.title: Efficient Dictionary Learning with Switch Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders efficiently to reduce compute cost while maintaining performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture that uses a mixture-of-experts style routing to reduce compute cost and memory bottlenecks while maintaining reconstruction performance and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Switch SAEs are a promising approach for scaling sparse autoencoders, providing a Pareto improvement in FLOPs vs. MSE without significant reduction in feature interpretability, and may enable large-scale SAE training on GPU clusters.
papers.key_findings:
Switch SAEs achieve better reconstruction than dense TopK SAEs at a fixed compute budget (FLOP-matched).
Switch SAEs require more total features (parameters) to achieve the same reconstruction as dense SAEs when trained to convergence, but this gap narrows for larger SAEs.
In FLOP-matched settings, Switch SAEs Pareto-dominate TopK, Gated, and ReLU SAEs in terms of reconstruction MSE and fraction of loss recovered.
Switch SAEs exhibit feature duplication across experts, which reduces capacity, but this effect diminishes at larger sparsities.
Switch SAE features are as interpretable as TopK SAE features in FLOP-matched settings, and in width-matched settings they have higher true positive rates but lower true negative rates in automated interpretability detection.
papers.limitation:
Switch SAEs have reduced performance at a fixed number of parameters compared to dense SAEs, especially for attention and MLP layers.
Only the simplest mixture-of-experts architecture is investigated, leaving open the question of maximum performance gain from more sophisticated MoE architectures.
No downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs (e.g., feature steering or circuit discovery) are conducted.
future_direction: Investigate feature deduplication techniques, more sophisticated routing architectures, and multiple active experts.
Explore more sophisticated mixture-of-experts architectures like GShard, DeepSeekMoE, and expert choice routing.
Conduct downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs, such as feature steering or circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a recent technique for decomposing neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, in order for SAEs to identify all features represented in frontier models, it will be necessary to scale them up to very high width, posing a computational challenge. In this work, we introduce Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture aimed at reducing the compute cost of training SAEs. Inspired by sparse mixture of experts models, Switch SAEs route activation vectors between smaller "expert" SAEs, enabling SAEs to efficiently scale to many more features. We present experiments comparing Switch SAEs with other SAE architectures, and find that Switch SAEs deliver a substantial Pareto improvement in the reconstruction vs. sparsity frontier for a given fixed training compute budget. We also study the geometry of features across experts, analyze features duplicated across experts, and verify that Switch SAE features are as interpretable as features found by other SAE architectures.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Antibody Language Models Using SAEs
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal interpretable features in antibody language models and be used to steer generation? How do TopK and Ordered SAEs compare in terms of interpretability and steerability?
papers.core_contribution: TopK SAEs can identify interpretable features in antibody language models but are not steerable, while Ordered SAEs can identify steerable features but with less interpretable activation patterns, suggesting Ordered SAEs are preferable for generative steering.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are effective for interpretability and steering in antibody language models, with trade-offs between interpretability and steerability between TopK and Ordered SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features in antibody language models.
High feature-concept correlation in TopK SAEs does not guarantee causal control over generation.
Ordered SAEs impose a hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features.
Ordered SAEs come at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns.
SAEs can be used to incorporate rational design principles into antibody library generation.
papers.limitation:
Lack of labelled datasets for antibodies compared to general proteins, which prevents automated feature identification and annotation.
TopK SAEs may not consistently generate monosemantic features for all concepts.
future_direction: Conduct exhaustive steering analyses to quantitatively measure the steerability of Top-K and Ordered SAE features.
Scale SAE training using more expansive, annotated datasets like FLAb to enable models to identify domain-specific abstractions.
Use SAEs to generate antibody libraries with properties such as developability and specificity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a mechanistic interpretability technique that have been used to provide insight into learned concepts within large protein language models. Here, we employ TopK and Ordered SAEs to investigate an autoregressive antibody language model, p-IgGen, and steer its generation. We show that TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features, but high feature concept correlation does not guarantee causal control over generation. In contrast, Ordered SAEs impose an hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features, but at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns. These findings advance the mechanistic interpretability of domain-specific protein language models and suggest that, while TopK SAEs are sufficient for mapping latent features to concepts, Ordered SAEs are preferable when precise generative steering is required.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: SynthSAEBench: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Scalable Realistic Synthetic Data
papers.research_question: How can we create a scalable synthetic benchmark with ground-truth features to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SynthSAEBench, a toolkit and benchmark for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics (correlation, hierarchy, superposition) to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures.
papers.conclusion: SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling precise diagnosis of SAE failure modes and validation of architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Reproduces LLM SAE phenomena: Matryoshka SAEs overperform on probing despite poor reconstruction; MP-SAEs overperform on reconstruction but poor probing; poor SAE probing relative to supervised probes; precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0.
Identifies a new failure mode: MP-SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting expressive encoders can overfit.
No SAE architecture achieves perfect performance on SynthSAEBench-16k, highlighting a target for architectural improvement.
papers.limitation: The synthetic model cannot capture all aspects of real neural network representations.
future_direction: Extend the framework to Minkowski representations and feature manifolds.
Understand the performance gap between JumpReLU and BatchTopK SAEs.
papers.abstract: Improving Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) requires benchmarks that can precisely validate architectural innovations. However, current SAE benchmarks on LLMs are often too noisy to differentiate architectural improvements, and current synthetic data experiments are too small-scale and unrealistic to provide meaningful comparisons. We introduce SynthSAEBench, a toolkit for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics including correlation, hierarchy, and superposition, and a standardized benchmark model, SynthSAEBench-16k, enabling direct comparison of SAE architectures. Our benchmark reproduces several previously observed LLM SAE phenomena, including the disconnect between reconstruction and latent quality metrics, poor SAE probing results, and a precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0. We further use our benchmark to identify a new failure mode: Matching Pursuit SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting that more expressive encoders can easily overfit. SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling researchers to precisely diagnose SAE failure modes and validate architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Interpretability Evals for Dictionary Learning Interpretability Evals Case Study Self-explaining SAE features
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the interpretability of dictionary learning features, and do new sparse autoencoder (SAE) variants improve interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs.
papers.conclusion: New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Eval and Sort eval provide measures of SAE feature interpretability that correlate with evaluation loss.
Non-vanilla SAE variants (TopK, Gated, Tanh, JumpReLU) perform better than vanilla SAEs on interpretability evals.
The self-explaining method via feature injection works well for early layer features but is less effective for complex concepts and larger models.
Interpretability evals can derisk the adoption of new SAE methods by providing quality metrics.
The evaluations are not comprehensive and measure only a single notion of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The evals are not comprehensive and only measure a single notion of interpretability, which is nebulous.
The evaluations likely do not have the resolution to distinguish small performance differences between SAE variants.
The self-explaining method succeeds less often on larger models and is sensitive to scale.
future_direction: Creating more and better evaluations for sparse autoencoders.
Using self-explaining techniques as complementary tools in interpretability.
papers.abstract: How can we evaluate the interpretability of dictionary learning features, and do new sparse autoencoder (SAE) variants improve interpretability? Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs. New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.

papers.title: Superior Molecular Representations from Intermediate Encoder Layers
papers.research_question: Are we overlooking superior molecular representations by adhering to the final-layer convention in chemistry? Specifically, do intermediate layers of molecular encoders provide more informative and task-relevant features for downstream property prediction than the final layer?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate layers of pretrained molecular encoders retain more general-purpose features and yield superior performance on downstream property prediction tasks compared to the final layer, both when used as frozen embeddings and when finetuned, leading to substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The common practice of relying solely on final-layer representations from pretrained molecular encoders is suboptimal; exploring intermediate layers yields substantial performance gains and computational savings, advocating for a shift beyond the final-layer default.
papers.key_findings:
Using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4% (up to 28.6%) compared to the final-layer, with 81% of model-task combinations preferring a non-final layer.
Finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves average improvements of 8.5% (up to 40.8%) over finetuning the complete encoder, with 71% of cases showing gains.
Label-free probes (tokenized-molecule entropy and adjacent-layer CKA) show that final layers undergo specialization and compression, while intermediate layers retain more transferable features.
The optimal intermediate layer varies by encoder architecture and downstream task; no single depth is universally best.
Frozen embedding performance correlates with finetuning performance (median Pearson correlation 0.60), providing an efficient proxy for selecting layers to finetune.
papers.limitation: The study is constrained by computational resources to five encoders and 22 ADMET tasks; extending the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains could further validate the findings.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains.
Conduct future work with additional architectures, multiple random seeds, and more exhaustive hyperparameter searches for deeper insights and more robust generalizations.
papers.abstract: Pretrained molecular encoders have become indispensable in computational chemistry for tasks such as property prediction and molecular generation. However, the standard practice of relying solely on final-layer embeddings for downstream tasks may discard valuable information. In this work, we first analyze the information flow in five diverse molecular encoders and find that intermediate layers retain more general-purpose features, whereas the final-layer specializes and compresses information. We then perform an empirical layer-wise evaluation across 22 property prediction tasks. We find that using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4%, up to 28.6%, compared to the final-layer. Furthermore, finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves even greater average improvements of 8.5%, with increases as high as 40.8%, obtaining new state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. These findings highlight the importance of exploring the full representational depth of molecular encoders to achieve substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Using attribution to decode binding mechanism in neural network models for chemistry
papers.research_question: Why do virtual screening models make the predictions they do? The paper aims to assess the influence of dataset biases on the prediction of protein binding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) to test hypotheses about binding logic and reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, showing that models can achieve perfect accuracy while learning spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods can reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, and models can be fooled by adversarial examples despite perfect accuracy. Practitioners should analyze model predictions and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on synthetic binding logics achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test sets but often have low attribution-AUC, indicating they learn spurious correlations.
Attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) can be used to identify dataset biases and construct adversarial examples that fool the model.
The attribution-AUC metric quantifies how well the model's attributions align with the hypothesized binding logic.
In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: OrtSAE: Orthogonal Sparse Autoencoders Uncover Atomic Features
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate feature absorption and composition in sparse autoencoders to learn more atomic, interpretable features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OrtSAE, a sparse autoencoder training method that enforces orthogonality between decoder features to reduce feature absorption and composition, yielding more atomic and interpretable features with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: OrtSAE effectively addresses feature absorption and composition in sparse autoencoders through orthogonal constraints, producing more atomic features while preserving reconstruction fidelity and downstream task performance with minimal computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
OrtSAE discovers 9% more distinct features than traditional SAEs.
OrtSAE reduces feature absorption by 65% and feature composition by 15% compared to traditional SAEs.
OrtSAE improves performance on spurious correlation removal by 6% while maintaining on-par performance on other downstream tasks.
OrtSAE achieves feature orthogonality near random initialization levels, significantly lower than other SAE variants.
OrtSAE decomposes composite features from traditional SAEs into more atomic components, as shown qualitatively.
future_direction: Investigate using orthogonal features as more interpretable building blocks for neural circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a technique for sparse decomposition of neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, current SAEs suffer from feature absorption, where specialized features capture instances of general features creating representation holes, and feature composition, where independent features merge into composite representations. In this work, we introduce Orthogonal SAE (OrtSAE), a novel approach aimed to mitigate these issues by enforcing orthogonality between the learned features. By implementing a new training procedure that penalizes high pairwise cosine similarity between SAE features, OrtSAE promotes the development of disentangled features while scaling linearly with the SAE size, avoiding significant computational overhead. We train OrtSAE across different models and layers and compare it with other methods. We find that OrtSAE discovers 9% more distinct features, reduces feature absorption (by 65%) and composition (by 15%), improves performance on spurious correlation removal (+6%), and achieves on-par performance for other downstream tasks compared to traditional SAEs.

papers.title: Exploiting Latent Linearity in LLMs Improves Explainable Molecular Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can LLM-derived molecular representations be linearly decomposed into chemically meaningful concepts (functional groups), and how can this latent linearity be exploited for explainable molecular property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MoleX, a framework that decomposes LLM latent representations into a concept-aligned space of functional groups and shows that a sparse linear mapping onto these chemical concepts improves both predictive accuracy and explainability for molecular property prediction.
papers.conclusion: Exploiting latent linearity in LLM representations provides a principled basis for effective and explainable molecular representation learning, improving accuracy, explainability, and efficiency in molecular property prediction.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-derived molecular representations exhibit latent linearity that can be expressed as a weighted combination of chemically meaningful functional group concepts.
MoleX outperforms existing GNN, LLM, and explainable machine learning baselines in predictive accuracy and explanation faithfulness on benchmark molecular property prediction tasks.
A residual calibration strategy corrects errors from the base linear predictor, further improving accuracy and explanation alignment with ground-truth substructures.
MoleX achieves significant computational efficiency, with CPU inference over 300x faster than LLMs and using 100,000 fewer parameters.
The linear predictor's performance scales with model size, training precision, and dataset size, but task-adapted training is crucial for converting capacity into performance gains.
papers.limitation: The linear predictor may underfit complex molecular patterns in some cases, as there is a trade-off between model complexity and performance.
future_direction: Examine the complexity–performance trade-off in LLM-based molecular representation learning to identify optimal balances between model complexity and downstream performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated broad utility across molecular domains, spanning drug discovery and materials design. Analyzing LLMs' latent representations is crucial for elucidating their underlying mechanisms, improving explainability, and ultimately advancing downstream performance. We propose MoleX, a simple yet effective framework that decomposes molecular embeddings within LLM representations into a concept-aligned space for explainable molecular representation learning. We further show that these high-dimensional embeddings admit a linear mapping onto chemically consistent concepts. Our analysis suggests that the uncovered linearity aligns with established chemical principles, indicating a mechanistically explainable latent structure in LLM representations for scientific applications. When applied to downstream tasks, this latent linearity improves both predictive and explanatory performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoleX outperforms existing approaches in accuracy, explainability, and efficiency, achieving CPU inference on large-scale datasets 300 times faster with 100,000 fewer parameters than LLMs.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: Understanding sparse autoencoder scaling in the presence of feature manifolds
papers.research_question: How do feature manifolds influence the scaling behavior of sparse autoencoders, and can they cause pathological scaling where SAEs allocate too many latents to common manifolds at the expense of discovering rarer features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts a capacity-allocation model to sparse autoencoders, revealing that feature manifolds can lead to pathological scaling where SAEs allocate excessive latents to common manifolds, potentially hindering feature discovery.
papers.conclusion: The work frames the problem of SAE scaling and identifies conditions for pathological scaling, but it remains uncertain whether real SAEs are in this regime due to unknown feature geometry and frequency distributions.
papers.key_findings:
The model recovers distinct scaling regimes for SAEs: one where feature discovery keeps pace with latent count, and another where latents accumulate on common feature manifolds.
When the per-feature loss scaling exponent β is less than the feature frequency exponent α, SAEs enter a pathological regime where they learn far fewer features than the number of latents.
Experiments on synthetic manifolds show that the loss scaling curve depends on manifold geometry; some manifolds allow gradual loss reduction with more latents, while others saturate quickly.
Analysis of real SAEs (Gemma Scope and Inception-v1) shows some latents with high cosine similarity, but evidence for pathological tiling is inconclusive.
The presence of radial variation in feature manifolds may cause SAEs to learn basis-like solutions rather than tiling, suggesting pathological scaling might not occur in practice.
papers.limitation:
The assumptions of feature-specific latents, decoder respect for subspaces, and orthogonal feature subspaces may not hold in practice (e.g., due to feature absorption and non-orthogonality).
The model assumes power-law distributions for feature frequencies and loss scaling, which may not accurately reflect real data.
The question of whether SAEs are in the pathological regime is not resolved due to uncertainty about real feature geometries and frequencies.
future_direction: Estimating the feature frequency exponent α and loss scaling exponent β for real SAEs.
Studying the geometry of real feature manifolds to better understand SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) model the activations of a neural network as linear combinations of sparsely occurring directions of variation (latents). The ability of SAEs to reconstruct activations follows scaling laws w.r.t. the number of latents. In this work, we adapt a capacity-allocation model from the neural scaling literature (Brill, 2024) to understand SAE scaling, and in particular, to understand how "feature manifolds" (multi-dimensional features) influence scaling behavior. Consistent with prior work, the model recovers distinct scaling regimes. Notably, in one regime, feature manifolds have the pathological effect of causing SAEs to learn far fewer features in data than there are latents in the SAE. We provide some preliminary discussion on whether or not SAEs are in this pathological regime in the wild.

papers.title: Probing the Representational Power of Sparse Autoencoders in Vision Models
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting and steering vision models, and do they provide semantically meaningful features across different vision architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs extract semantically meaningful features from vision models, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable semantic steering in diffusion models, establishing SAEs as a valuable interpretability tool for vision.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are semantically meaningful and enhance interpretable understanding across vision encoders, multimodal LLMs, and diffusion models, highlighting SAEs as a unified interpretability tool across diverse vision architectures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features from vision encoders improve out-of-distribution generalization compared to original embeddings.
SAE features capture hierarchical semantic structures (ontological features) in image encoders.
SAEs enable semantic steering in diffusion models by manipulating text encoder features.
SAEs reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities in LMMs.
Different SAE variants (ReLU, TopK, Gated) show similar trends in reconstruction and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Findings on multimodal representation overlap in LMMs are preliminary and require future quantitative validation.
Steering Stable Diffusion 3.5 is more challenging due to its complex text encoding architecture.
future_direction: Quantitative validation of multimodal representation overlap in LMMs.
Systematic investigation of how visual representations evolve through LLM layers.
Future application of SAEs in vision models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a popular tool for interpreting the hidden states of large language models (LLMs). By learning to reconstruct activations from a sparse bottleneck layer, SAEs discover interpretable features from the high-dimensional internal representations of LLMs. Despite their popularity with language models, SAEs remain understudied in the visual domain. In this work, we provide an extensive evaluation the representational power of SAEs for vision models using a broad range of image-based tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SAE features are semantically meaningful, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable controllable generation across three vision model architectures: vision embedding models, multi-modal LMMs and diffusion models. In vision embedding models, we find that learned SAE features can be used for OOD detection and provide evidence that they recover the ontological structure of the underlying model. For diffusion models, we demonstrate that SAEs enable semantic steering through text encoder manipulation and develop an automated pipeline for discovering human-interpretable attributes. Finally, we conduct exploratory experiments on multi-modal LLMs, finding evidence that SAE features reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities. Our study provides a foundation for SAE evaluation in vision models, highlighting their strong potential improving interpretability, generalization, and steerability in the visual domain.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: SAE-RNA: A Sparse Autoencoder Model for Interpreting RNA Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How and what do RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-RNA, a sparse autoencoder model that interprets RNA language model representations by discovering sparse features aligned with biological structures and ncRNA families.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RNA provides a method for concept discovery in pretrained RNA LM embeddings, enabling interpretation without retraining and offering features for downstream tasks like feature-aware fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features localize in structurally meaningful regions such as stems and hairpins.
Features exhibit sequence biases like poly-G/C/A/U tracts that map onto secondary-structure contexts.
Deeper layers transition from diffuse to type-selective activations, with a small subset of channels preferentially firing for specific ncRNA families.
The last layer shows diminished signal, suggesting late-stage representational compression.
Features can be annotated using LLM prompting to align with known biological motifs.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints restricted the scale of training data used for the SAE models.
SAE training outcomes can vary depending on hyperparameter choices, such as sparsity setting, which may influence the granularity and stability of learned features.
future_direction: Feature-aware fine-tuning with SAE-derived features for downstream RNA tasks.
papers.abstract: Deep learning, particularly with the advancement of Large Language Models, has transformed biomolecular modeling, with protein advances (e.g., ESM) inspiring emerging RNA language models such as RiNALMo. Yet how and what these RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families remains unclear. We present SAE- RNA, interpretability model that analyzes RiNALMo representations and maps them to known human-level biological features. Our work frames RNA interpretability as concept discovery in pretrained embeddings, without end-to-end retraining, and provides practical tools to probe what RNA LMs may encode about ncRNA families. The model can be extended to close comparisons between RNA groups, and supporting hypothesis generation about previously unrecognized relationships.

papers.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable monosemantic features from polysemantic activations in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes PS-Eval, a new evaluation metric and dataset for assessing whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations. It finds that SAEs optimized for MSE-L0 Pareto frontier do not necessarily improve monosemantic feature extraction, and that deeper layers and attention mechanisms contribute to distinguishing polysemous words.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes Poly-Semantic Evaluation (PS-Eval), a new metric and dataset to assess the ability of SAEs to extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations, in complement to traditional MSE or L0 metrics. The work encourages the community to conduct holistic evaluations of SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability and do not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features.
Deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word.
Increasing the latent dimension of SAEs generally improves specificity up to a saturation point.
Activation functions like TopK and JumpReLU, designed to improve MSE-L0 trade-off, do not perform well on PS-Eval metrics; ReLU performs best.
SAE features are more interpretable than raw LLM activations for polysemous words.
papers.limitation: PS-Eval relies on evaluating the maximum activation of SAE features, which may not always align with intended word meanings and could introduce ambiguity.
future_direction: Incorporate similarity metrics that utilize the distribution of SAE features, rather than relying solely on maximum activation.
Extend PS-Eval beyond natural language to other domains such as diffusion models and vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have gained a lot of attention as a promising tool to improve the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) by mapping the complex superposition of polysemantic neurons into monosemantic features and composing a sparse dictionary of words. However, traditional performance metrics like Mean Squared Error and L0 sparsity ignore the evaluation of the semantic representational power of SAEs -- whether they can acquire interpretable monosemantic features while preserving the semantic relationship of words. For instance, it is not obvious whether a learned sparse feature could distinguish different meanings in one word. In this paper, we propose a suite of evaluations for SAEs to analyze the quality of monosemantic features by focusing on polysemous words. Our findings reveal that SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability, which does not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features. The analysis of SAEs with polysemous words can also figure out the internal mechanism of LLMs; deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word. Our semantics focused evaluation offers new insights into the polysemy and the existing SAE objective and contributes to the development of more practical SAEs.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Don't Forget It! Conditional Sparse Autoencoder Clamping Works for Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders be used to unlearn harmful knowledge in large language models while retaining safe knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a conditional SAE-based clamping method for unlearning that improves retention of safe information compared to prior SAE methods and performs comparably to RMU with better interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning outperforms prior SAE approaches on retention and performs comparably with RMU on forgetting harmful information while retaining safe information, with fewer hyperparameters and better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal Clamp achieves the lowest WMDP-bio accuracy (0.2718) and highest alignment score (0.8226), indicating effective unlearning with some impact on general knowledge.
Clamp Prime improves forgetting performance (WMDP-bio accuracy drops to 0.2985) but slightly reduces general knowledge retention compared to RMU.
Adversarial evaluation using Concurrent Greedy Search shows that unlearned models resist suffix attacks, continuing to output gibberish.
The method requires fewer hyperparameter choices than RMU while maintaining interpretability.
